catalog_quote: [Abstract] Little research has examined the temporal alignment of co-speech gestures in African tonal languages, where metrical prominence is often hard to identify due to a lack of canonical stress correlates, and where a key function of pitch is in distinguishing between words, rather than marking intonational prominence. ... the final syllable in the word is the default position for gesture alignment in Igbo ... [sec. 1] As is the case for most Niger-Congo languages (particularly those situated in the northwestern region of Sub-Saharan Africa), neither of these languages displays typical acoustic correlates of lexical stress, such as increased vowel duration or intensity. Nonetheless, for both languages, there is some evidence to suggest that word-level metrical prominence asymmetries are present (Clark 1990; Franich 2018, 2021). ... tone is primarily used to encode lexical contrasts…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Igbo (nucl1417) is not in the catalog. Of the five title-hit items, only Anyanwu 2003 'Tone and accent in the Igbo verb' (FAB 15, Köppe; publisher-sold PDF, no DOI, no open copy anywhere I could reach: HathiTrust ISBN lookup empty, archive.org empty, Frankfurt server 403) is squarely about accent placement in Igbo words — high priority, unread. Zsiga 1992 (CUP paywall; abstract read via Crossref) is about prosodic domains via ATR harmony and vowel assimilation, not stress; her open 1997 Language paper on the same rules was downloaded and is silent on stress. Uzochukwu 1981 is verse metre (T&F paywall, no abstract exposed; low). Manfredi 1992 IRCS (held by the project, read) is downstep/downstep-reset in Àgbọ̀ Igbo under a tone-metrical government model — silent on word stress. Ezeriọha 2014 (UNN MA thesis, 101 pp.) could not be located (repository unreachable). Best first-hand statement actually read: Franich, Keupdjio & Nwosu 2025 (Glossa, held by the project) — Igbo shows no acoustic correlates of lexical stress; word-level metrical prominence, per Clark 1990 and the authors' gesture data, is word-final (right-to-left alternating); Franich & Nwosu 2026 (LabPhon) restates Clark's analysis. Clark 1990 (De Gruyter) remains the unread primary source, high priority. DDG, Bing, Brave, Mojeek, Google Scholar, HathiTrust and T&F pages bot-blocked), so discovery relied on Crossref, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Glottolog, Köppe and author sites.

new_statements.quote: [p.1] Little research has examined the temporal alignment of co-speech gestures in African tonal languages, where metrical prominence is often hard to identify due to a lack of canonical stress correlates ... the final syllable in the word is the default position for gesture alignment in Igbo ... [p.9] Specifically, she [Clark 1990] proposes that the language assigns alternating prominences from the right edge of the word, and that initial metrically-prominent syllables actually resist the linking of the associative high tone ... [p.27] In Igbo, on the other hand, word-final position is the strongest attractor of gestures. This finding is in line with work by Clark (1990) arguing for the right-to-left assignment of metrical prominences at the word level in Igbo.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (39 pp., Glossa 10(1), CC-BY 4.0, text layer present; alongside). All three quoted stretches are present verbatim at the stated locators: (p.1, abstract) 'Little research has examined the temporal alignment of co-speech gestures in African tonal languages, where metrical prominence is often hard to identify due to a lack of canonical stress correlates.. the final syllable in the word is the default position for gesture alignment in Igbo'; (printed p.9, sec. 1.2) 'Specifically, she proposes that the language assigns alternating prominences from the right edge of the word, and that initial metrically-prominent syllables actually resist the linking of the associative high tone (a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Igbo is a two-tone (H, L + downstep) language with no canonical acoustic stress correlates; the only word-prominence claim is metrical: Clark (1990) assigns alternating prominence right-to-left so the word-final syllable is prominent (and the initial syllable of trisyllables), and Franich et al.'s co-speech-gesture timing data independently pick out the word-final syllable as the default prominent position. No source opened states a conventional word-stress rule; the standard descriptive grammars (Emenanjo 2015, Green & Igwe 1963) could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Clark's analysis (as reported) implies alternating prominence leftward from the final syllable, i.e. initial syllable of trisyllabic words also metrically strong; Franich et al. additionally suggest a left-edge prominence at the start of a multiply-linked H tone span ('tonal foot').
new_statements.exceptions: Words with HH melody (single multiply-linked H) attract gestures to the initial syllable more often; prominence/gesture shifts leftward when the word-final vowel undergoes coalescence/reduction in hiatus (Franich & Nwosu 2026 'gesture shift'); phrase position also modulates alignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level metrical prominence inferred from tonal phonology (downstep resistance in the associative construction) and from gesture-apex alignment in spontaneous interview speech (4 speakers, greater Abuja area); not citation-form stress and not an acoustic stress study. Clark 1990's own wording was not seen (second-hand via these papers).
new_statements.identity_note: Franich et al.'s Igbo data come from four speakers recorded in the greater Abuja area (variety not specified beyond 'Igbo'; examples follow Standard Igbo forms); Clark 1990's analysis is of Standard/Central Igbo (her 1978 data largely Ohuhu/Owerri-area per Green & Igwe tradition). Manfredi 1992 concerns Agbo (Ika area, cf. Glottolog ikaa1238 'Ika'), which Glottolog treats as a separate Igboid language, so it was not used for the statement. Older Ganot 1899 describes Onitsha-area Igbo.

new_statements.citation: Franich, Kathryn, Hermann Keupdjio & Vincent Nwosu (2025). The timing of speech and gesture in two Niger-Congo languages: Implications for word-level prominence. Glossa 10(1): 1-39. doi:10.16995/glossa.17426

new_statements.reading: Igbo is a tone language with no lexical stress in the usual acoustic sense (no stress-related duration or intensity); the only word-level prominence claimed is an abstract metrical one, defaulting to the word-final syllable with alternating prominences leftward (Clark 1990), which the authors' own gesture-alignment data support. For a stress catalog this reads as 'no word stress / tone language', with a documented word-final metrical-prominence analysis as a secondary note.

sources.note: First-hand experimental statement: Igbo has no canonical acoustic correlates of lexical stress (no duration/intensity stress); word-level metrical prominence, diagnosed by downstep resistance (Clark 1990) and by co-speech gesture alignment in the authors' own data, defaults to the word-final syllable (right-to-left alternating), modulated by tone melody and phrase position.

sources.locator: Abstract p. 1; sec. 1.2 p. 9; sec. 4 Discussion p. 27
sources.note: African tone languages such as Igbo lack canonical stress correlates; restates Clark (1990): Igbo assigns alternating metrical prominences from the right edge of the word (word-final syllable prominent; initial syllable of trisyllables also prominent, which resists associative-H docking/downstep); own co-speech-gesture data (4 speakers, Abuja area): word-final syllable is the default/strongest gesture-attracting (prominent) position; tone value itself not a strong determinant; a second left-edge 'tonal foot' prominence also suggested.

sources.quote: Clark interprets this difference in behavior across the two types of nouns as related to their underlying metrical structures. She proposes that metrical prominence at the word level is assigned from right to left, with metrical prominence assigned to word-final syllables and alternating syllables moving leftward. The initial metrically prominent syllable in a trisyllabic word allows it to resist the tone docking that would trigger downstep in the associative construction.
sources.note: Sec. 1.4 (pp. 7-8): per Clark (1990) 'metrical prominence at the word level is assigned from right to left, with metrical prominence assigned to word-final syllables and alternating syllables moving leftward'; gesture evidence for word-final metrical status; prominence can shift leftward when the final vowel reduces/coalesces ('gesture shift').

sources.quote: In a framework of tone-metrical licensing (Bamba 1992, Manfredi 1992), the two downstep-reset contexts share one property: a H tone in a weak position. The configurations which predict weak H are found in surface syntax. Weak H also accounts for downstep-reset in the Ábánkeleke dialect—previously claimed to have a so-called 'upstep' juncture—and in standard Ìgbo.
sources.note: About downstep and downstep-reset ('antidownstep') in the Àgbọ̀ (Agbor) variety of Igbo, analysed with a tone-metrical government model (H > L > M as metrical governors; strong/weak positions licensed by syntax). 'Metrical' here means tonal government relations, not word stress. The word 'stress' occurs only in the bibliography (Liberman & Prince 1977). Silent on word stress.

sources.quote: Igbo presents just such a mismatch. This paper will examine two rules – ATR vowel harmony and vowel assimilation – that make the mismatch clear. These two rules apply in complementary situations: harmony applies only within the word, assimilation only between words. Both rules delineate the same domain, although one operates within the domain boundaries, one across them.
sources.note: Abstract: about prosodic domains (phonological word) as delineated by ATR harmony (word-internal) and vowel assimilation (across words); nothing on stress or accent. CUP paywall; Unpaywall reports no OA copy; not on the author's publications page (zsigae.com). The author's open 1997 Language paper on the same Igbo vowel rules (downloaded, see separate item) is silent on stress, so the 1992 paper is very unlikely to state a stress rule.
